claims.text: A higher grain-boundary density lowers the local kinetic barrier for atomic rearrangement in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Grain boundaries serve as nucleation sites for premelting and melting.
Increasing grain-boundary density causes an earlier onset of premelting and melting.
Increasing grain-boundary density makes the phase transition more spatially heterogeneous.
Rapid quenching will maximize grain-boundary defect density relative to post-synthesis annealing.
Post-synthesis annealing will reduce grain-boundary defect density.
High-resolution imaging and diffraction can isolate grain-boundary contributions from other defect types.
Grain boundaries are energetically favorable sites for nucleation of a liquid-like phase.
Grain boundaries locally reduce the melting point.
A liquid-like phase first forms at grain-boundary defects and then propagates through the nanoparticle.
Defect-initiated liquid propagation accelerates premelting and heterogeneous melting.
High-grain-boundary-density nanoparticles will have a measurably lower premelting onset temperature than annealed low-boundary-density nanoparticles.
High-grain-boundary-density nanoparticles will show localized liquid-phase formation at defect sites.
The annealed low-defect-density batch represents normal melting behavior without enhanced defect-induced nucleation.
Holding composition, crystallographic parameters, environment, and thermal ramp constant would make grain-boundary density the sole source of observed differences.
Changing cooling and annealing histories may inadvertently change other defects or microstructural factors that influence melting.
Statistically similar premelting onset temperatures together with no preferential localized melting at grain boundaries would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The boundary statement says the controls ensure that observed differences stem solely from grain-boundary density, while the uncertainty statement acknowledges that cooling-rate and annealing changes may alter other defects or microstructural factors that affect melting.
